Yandisa, the penguin and seabird ranger

By: Annalise Lubbe | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We get a unique glimpse into the life of a female ranger who lives with hundreds of penguins and seabirds on an island whom most of us only remember as a maximum security prison.

Unique Selling Point:
Meet Yandisa Cwecwe, Robben Island’s very own penguin and seabird ranger. She has a full time job looking after more than 900 African penguins nesting on the island.

Yandisa is the only penguin and seabird ranger stationed on Robben island but from time to time environmentalists and scientists visit the penguin colony to conduct fieldwork and check if the equipment to monitor the penguins’ moves are fully functional.



Summary:
Robben island is situated 11 km from Cape Town harbour. It was declared a marine protected area in 2019 and is managed by Table Mountain National Park. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site best known for its iconic landmark: the maximum security prison where Nelson Mandela and other political prisoners were incarcerated during apartheid. Other iconic landmarks include the Robben Island lighthouse (built in 1864) and relics from WWII when the island was an important military base.

But few people know about the penguin colony and for good reason: it is strictly out of bounds for visitors and only a select few are invited to spend a day with these endearing birds in the company of their full time ranger, Yandisa.

Yandisa grew up in Lusikisiki in the Eastern Cape, 45 km from the sea. Her interest in marine life and its creatures was sparked during a life-changing visit to a marine protected area along the Eastern Cape Wild Coast. After completing her degree in Zoology she specialised in marine biology. After graduating she worked under the National Research Foundation as a research assistant intern for two years in a Marine Conservation Genomics laboratory at Stellenbosch University before taking up a post at the Southern African Foundation for the Conservation of Coastal Birds (SANCCOB).

“My passion and love for the African penguins really began here at SANCCOB where I first worked as a researcher. When the position of ranger became available I immediately applied. I wanted to be on the ground, close to the penguins and other seabirds and to see where they are being rescued. I also wanted to contribute towards the efforts of conserving marine life, especially the endangered African penguin”, says Yandisa.

Yandisa’s passion and dedication for her work is evident. Monitoring over a thousand breeding pairs of penguins is no mean feat. Crawling on all fours to check in on the conditions of the newborn chicks or rescuing sick or injured birds, it is all part of a day’s job.

“We are always monitoring the chicks on the island especially for being underweight. Penguin food sources have diminished so much due to the overfishing of sardines and anchovies that penguin parents must travel far distances to find food, often leaving their chicks alone for very long periods of time, sometimes not making it back at all. This makes the chicks and eggs vulnerable to predators, bad weather and starvation”, says Yandisa.

On average, 500 - 600 African penguin chicks and 300 to 400 African penguin eggs are brought to SANCCOB chick rearing facility at Table Bay each year by rangers from across the 6 penguin colonies with numbers increasing by 256% in the last seven years. The numbers speak for themselves. Abandoned chicks are on the increase and efforts of rangers like Yandisa are critical to the survival of the African penguin.

Robben Island is a hotspot for seabird biodiversity, including endangered cape cormorants, bank cormorants and African penguins. It lies in the middle of major shipping lanes, and the risk of oil spills to local seabirds has been well documented.

Dr Katta Ludynia, renowned marine biologist, with a Phd spearheads the research department at SANCCOB. She was Yandisa’s mentor whilst being an intern at SANCCOB before she was appointed penguin ranger on Robben Island. She saw Yandisa’s potential if given a chance to prove herself as a ranger and she wasn't disappointed. Katta frequently visits the island to see how the penguins are doing and to see how they can improve the monitoring systems and tools they have in their disposal.

The research conducted on the island is critical as it examines the consequences of fishing activities on African penguins and other seabirds’ population dynamics. The research contributes valuable data on the condition of South African seabirds admitted for rehabilitation. Sick or injured birds and abandoned chicks get sent to the mainland Chick Rearing facility where they are then rehabilitated. Shared with research institutions like Earthwatch - an international charity environmental group, these findings play a crucial role in shaping conservation efforts. As part of the national transponder project led by SANCCOB, all released birds are equipped with transponders.

For Yandisa, this has been a great two weeks, having enthusiastic people to share her passion with. “The most important thing for me is that I want to contribute towards the efforts of saving endangered marine life especially the african penguins so that is what keeps me going and my passion and love for nature”, says Yandisa.

The story:
The story is about Yandisa, the penguin ranger and her dedication to help save the penguins. Dr Katta Ludynia, marine biologist working closely with Yandisa will also be on the island to share her concerns for the dwindling penguin population and how they are pulling out all the stops to help preserve this seabird from extinction. We will check the monitoring tools which read the transponders implanted in the penguins, weigh and measure a chicks, check the nests and look for any abandoned chicks or eggs. Katta will also talk about the longstanding penguin project on Robben Island and how the research has given insight into the penguins’ behavioural patterns.

We will stay overnight on the island to get early morning and later afternoon shots of the penguins as they go out to sea to forage and return to land to feed their chicks. It is a personal narrative of the penguin ranger and how she spends her life on the island. The science then is a layer on top of that. It becomes more impactful to talk about the impact of climate change, man-made, and the current state of affairs with the penguin population if we have the personal narrative that the viewers can attach themselves to. From thousands of penguins to less than 900 breeding pairs is the reality we face on Robben Island, once the largest breeding colony. Food scarcity, oil pollution and climate change (rise in temperatures, storms, nests flooded) have all contributed.

Interviews:
Yandisa Cwecwe - Penguin and seabird ranger
Dr Katta Ludynia - Marine biologist



Further information:
According to reports from the 1600’s, African penguins were once abundant on Robben Island. However by 1800, they faced so much exploitation and disturbance - primarily for food, clothing, and oil by the early European settlers at the Cape - that they no longer bred there. Not until 1983 did African penguins begin to recolonise Robben Island. After that, the colony grew spectacularly, reaching over 8,000 breeding pairs in 2004 and was briefly the second-largest African penguin colony in the world in 2007.

Unfortunately, the story doesn’t end with the penguins’ recovery: the population has declined again. Human activity, such as oil spills and fishing, disturbs their habitat. Not only that, changes in ocean conditions, attributable to the effects of climate change, and the lack of sardine and anchovy - the penguins’ primary food resources - have seen the population plummeting to 1007 breeding pairs. As a result of these collective threats and the continued decline of the penguin populations, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) now classifies the species as Critically Endangered. Decreasing at 7.9% of their population a year, at that rate they could be extinct by 2035.

Script:


Final script: Yandisa, the penguin and seabird ranger

Up sound netball scene with Yandisa

VO1 A dimly lit netball court that could be anywhere in the country. But, while it might not look like much, it’s in a very unique place.

Upsound playing

And one of these players is at the frontline of the battle to save a critically endangered species.

Fade to black
Aerial shots Robben island

VO2 Robben Island: it’s a quaint landscape with a well-known history. Less familiar is the island’s role as a home to one of only six breeding colonies of African penguins in the country,
And 29 year-old Yandisa Cwecwe is their guardian.

Yandisa Cwecwe: Penguin Ranger - SANCCOB: I studied marine biology and I’d never seen penguins before until I moved to Cape Town. So I fell in love with them. They are cute but they are feisty.

VO3 Overfishing and climate change are having a significant impact on penguin numbers. Worldwide, only 14 000 remain.

Yandisa Cwecwe: Around 2007 we had more than 5000 breeding pairs on the island. And now we are sitting at 923 breeding pairs.

VO4: Without help, the African penguin could be extinct in the next decade.

Change of pace

VO5 It’s Monday morning at Cape Town Harbour and we’re waiting to board the ferry. We’ve been given a unique opportunity: to spend a night on the island with Yandisa and her penguins.

Up sound - Morning, hello

LINK: We are so lucky to be on this ferry. They can be canceled at a moment’s notice if the weather turns bad but it is a beautiful spring day and it is time to hop on board.

VO6 Onboard with us is Dr Katta Ludynia, a senior researcher at the Southern African Foundation for the Conservation of Coastal Birds, or SANCCOB, with a special interest in the African penguin.

Erin Bates: Katta, you have been studying penguins on the island for years. What are you noticing the impact is on the population decline?

Dr Katta Ludynia: Senior Researcher: The main issue we are currently facing is a lack of food. So these penguins feed exclusively on sardines and anchovies and those stocks are really depleted and at the same time they are also competing directly with the industrial fisheries for the same species.

Aerial shot of Robben Island over the houses

VO7: Robben Island is home to about one-hundred-and-fifty people: museum staff, ex-political prisoners working as tour guides… and occasional visiting researchers. There’s a small church, a curio shop, a scattering of houses… and not much else.

Arriving on the island
Erin Bates: Hello, I’m Erin
Yandisa Cwecwe: I’m Yandisa,
Erin Bates: Thanks for having us. So we are going to walk to your house?
Yandisa Cwecwe: No
Erin Bates: So there’s a bakkie waiting for us.

Aerial view driving shot to get a wider perspective

VO8 First we head to the penguin colony, where Katta and Yandisa check the monitoring equipment. Most penguins on the island are microchipped.

Erin Bates: So how does it work?

Katta Ludynia: So when a penguin has one of these chips, walks over one of these readers it basically just gets detected and it gets uploaded to a database. And then we can actually go back onto the database and we can see that the bird that walked over on Sunday morning at 7h00 is a bird that was rescued from Simonstown, hand-reared at SANCCOB, released at Stony Point in 2019 and it is now clearly on Robben Island.

VO9 The researchers use this data to track the penguin’s numbers - which are declining rapidly.

LINK: Robben island, like Antarctica, Siberia and several other parts of the world is a window into climate change and its impact. Here the toll of global warming can be felt and seen in the declining number of penguins.
slight pause
VO10 Once in their thousands, now on the brink of extinction.

Erin Bates: Can you talk about how climate change has affected the penguin?

Katta Ludynia: Yah, so climate change has quite a variety of impacts. For example we see these heavy winter storms and rains, these big flooding events we had this year for example, but we also see more and more of these heat waves.

Yandisa Cwecwe: So the penguins, when it's stormy, it's rainy, some of the nests get flooded so the penguins would leave their nests and then abandon their chicks, they also abandon the eggs.

VO11 This is where Yandisa comes in. She’s the boots on the ground when floods and storms hit. She rescues abandoned eggs and sends them to SANCCOB on the mainland, where the chicks are hand-reared until they’re old enough to be released back onto the island.

Change music: Yandisa picks up her clipboard; gumboots, jacket, walks to bakkie and drives off.

VO12: It’s a daily routine. Yandisa knows every nest on the island, and she visits all the residents to check on the health of breeding adults and their chicks.

Walking towards the burrow

VO13 She keeps a watch for sick and injured birds: every penguin is precious.

Yandisa Cwecwe: So last week I rescued two penguins. The other one was a chick that was underweight and the other one was an adult that was limping. And that adult was nesting and that means it was not able to go to sea to find food for its chicks.
…..The other nest I found was an exposed nest so the chicks were wet and freezing. So I had to find brush cut branches and put some cover to protect them. When I went back to check the nest again in the intense rain I found the chicks nice and warm.

Erin Bates: So you knew you done well. What’s that feeling like?

Yandisa Cwecwe: Like it's a good feeling. It’s a nice feeling. And I followed that nest until the chicks fledged.
Up sound

VO14: I tried my hands to scan a parent sitting on two eggs.
UP sound
Erin Bates: Mamma!
Yandisa Cwecwe: So before they fledge, we try to catch them and tag them. Don’t mind him, go again
UP Beeps sound
Erin Bates: There we go. Ok so it’s 11h22. Last three digits 985
Yandisa Cwecwe: 985. So it’s a different bird this week. So the other partner is out foraging.

VO15: Competition with commercial fishing boats means adults often can’t find enough food at sea. Yandisa measures the weight and size of the chicks to check they’re getting enough to eat.

Yandisa Cwecwe: This is how we hold the chicks because they are still small, we don't want to grab them by their flippers or their legs because they are still fragile. Make sure the chick is away from the face because they can sometimes bite.

Erin Bates: Here we go. For the first time I’m holding a penguin. Hello.
And how old do you think this one is?

Yandisa Cwecwe: It’s two to three weeks old.

VO16: Facing starvation, some adults simply abandon their nests. The rest are forced to travel further and further in search of food.

UP sound . Erin and Yandisa spots a tortoise “not quite a penguin”

VO17 We head to the beach hoping to spot adult penguins returning to land after a long day’s fishing.

Yandisa warns us to keep well clear, so we set up our cameras at a distance…and wait.

But before heading back to the house, we spot just one penguin reaching shore.
Disappointed, we head home for a coffee.

Up seagulls sound

Erin Bates: Do you feel any connection with the political history of the island?

Yandisa Cwecwe: Yah. I took that as a privilege for me to get to robben island and there are still ex political prisoners that still stay on the island that do the prisoner tours. So it’s nice to chat with people that can chat about their experiences.

VO18 And while some of her neighbours keep the political legacy alive, Yandisa fights to save its natural heritage ... .sometimes sneaking in a game of netball before bed.

Up netball sound

VO19 It’s 6:30 AM and we’re hoping for better luck today. Camera one, under the bushes and camera two is on the beach……on the lookout for penguins heading out to sea to hunt.

LINK: We got up at first light, set up two cameras and hid in the bushes waiting. It’s an hour later and we’ve only seen two penguins.
Cameraman: Yah, there they are.

VO20: Seeing so few hunting adults brought the harsh truth home for us: there aren’t many African penguins left… and the survivors travel so far for food that many don’t return by the end of the day… or ever.

LINK: I want to show you something unreal in Yandisa’s house. This is a snapshot of the penguin population in 1931. Tens of thousands of them and forecasts are that are that in just 11 years from now the entire world could be wiped of the African penguin population.

Pause

Yandisa Cwecwe: So that is why even if it is cold or raining, I go out there to make sure the penguins are fine because I don’t want them to go extinct so that our future generations can also see them.
_____________________________________________________________________________________________
Promos:
Promo 1: 21 seconds

V/O She came from the Eastern Cape and ended up on an island.

Yandisa Cwecwe: I’d never seen penguins before until I moved to CT. So I fell in love with them. They’re cute but they are feisty.

V/O With big boots to fill, she is the only ranger taking care of hundreds of African penguins.
_________________________________________________________________________
Promo 2: 21 seconds

V/O She is the only ranger on Robben island, looking after the African penguins.

Yandisa Cwecwe: Even if it is cold or raining, I go out there to make sure the penguins are fine because I don’t want them to go extinct in future.

V/O Heat waves, floods, and lack of food could drive the African penguin population to extinction in 2035.
____________________________________________________________________________

Promo 3: 21 seconds

V/O Climate change is staring us in the face…

Dr Katta Ludynia: The African penguin is part of an ecosystem, we see less chicks returning, we see them returning with less food, we see their chicks starving…so obviously something is going really wrong.

V/O By 2035 the African penguin species could be wiped out from the face of the earth.
__________________________________________________________________________

SUNDAY PROMO:
Up sound: Dr Katta Ludynia: The African penguin is showing us something is wrong, we see less chicks returning, we see them returning with less food, we see their chicks starving…

Erin Bates: This chick is only about three weeks old and the future looks precarious.

Up sound: Yandisa: When it's stormy, it's rainy, some of the nests get flooded so the penguins would leave their nests and then abandon their chicks there, they also abandon the eggs.

Erin Bates: The survival of its entire species hangs in the balance.

MORE OPTIONS FOR UPSOUNDS:

Up sound: Yandisa Cwecwe: Around 2007 we had more than 5000 breeding pairs on the island. And now we are sitting at 923 breeding pairs.

Up sound: Dr Katta Ludynia: We've done some modeling and the modeling shows that the species could be extinct by 2035 which is about ten years from now so that is very scary.

Up sound: Yandisa Cwecwe: So that is why even if it is cold or raining, that's' why I go out there to make sure the penguins are fine because I don’t want them to go extinct in future

Fade to black Aerial shots Robben island VO2 Robben Island: it’s a quaint landscape with a well-known history. Less familiar is the island’s role as a home to one of only six breeding colonies of African penguins in the country, And 29 year-old Yandisa Cwecwe is their guardian. Yandisa Cwecwe: Penguin Ranger - SANCCOB: I studied marine biology and I’d never seen penguins before until I moved to Cape Town. So I fell in love with them. They are cute but they are feisty. VO3 Overfishing and climate change are having a significant impact on penguin numbers. Worldwide, only 14 000 remain. Yandisa Cwecwe: Around 2007 we had more than 5000 breeding pairs on the island. Up sound - Morning, hello LINK: We are so lucky to be on this ferry. They can be canceled at a moment’s notice if the weather turns bad but it is a beautiful spring day and it is time to hop on board. VO6 Onboard with us is Dr Katta Ludynia, a senior researcher at the Southern African Foundation for the Conservation of Coastal Birds, or SANCCOB, with a special interest in the African penguin. Erin Bates: Katta, you have been studying penguins on the island for years. What are you noticing the impact is on the population decline? Dr Katta Ludynia: Senior Researcher: The main issue we are currently facing is a lack of food. So these penguins feed exclusively on sardines and anchovies and those stocks are really depleted and at the same time they are also competing directly with the industrial fisheries for the same species. Aerial shot of Robben Island over the houses VO7: Robben Island is home to about one-hundred-and-fifty people: museum staff, ex-political prisoners working as tour guides… and occasional visiting researchers. There’s a small church, a curio shop, a scattering of houses… and not much else. Arriving on the island Erin Bates: Hello, I’m Erin Yandisa Cwecwe: I’m Yandisa, Erin Bates: Thanks for having us. So we are going to walk to your house? Yandisa Cwecwe: No Erin Bates: So there’s a bakkie waiting for us. Aerial view driving shot to get a wider perspective VO8 First we head to the penguin colony, where Katta and Yandisa check the monitoring equipment. Most penguins on the island are microchipped. Erin Bates: So how does it work? Katta Ludynia: So when a penguin has one of these chips, walks over one of these readers it basically just gets detected and it gets uploaded to a database. And then we can actually go back onto the database and we can see that the bird that walked over on Sunday morning at 7h00 is a bird that was rescued from Simonstown, hand-reared at SANCCOB, released at Stony Point in 2019 and it is now clearly on Robben Island. VO9 The researchers use this data to track the penguin’s numbers - which are declining rapidly. LINK: Robben island, like Antarctica, Siberia and several other parts of the world is a window into climate change and its impact. Here the toll of global warming can be felt and seen in the declining number of penguins. slight pause VO10 Once in their thousands, now on the brink of extinction. Erin Bates: Can you talk about how climate change has affected the penguin? Katta Ludynia: Yah, so climate change has quite a variety of impacts. For example we see these heavy winter storms and rains, these big flooding events we had this year for example, but we also see more and more of these heat waves. Yandisa Cwecwe: So the penguins, when it's stormy, it's rainy, some of the nests get flooded so the penguins would leave their nests and then abandon their chicks, they also abandon the eggs. Change music: Yandisa picks up her clipboard; gumboots, jacket, walks to bakkie and drives off. VO12: It’s a daily routine. Yandisa knows every nest on the island, and she visits all the residents to check on the health of breeding adults and their chicks. Walking towards the burrow VO13 She keeps a watch for sick and injured birds: every penguin is precious. Yandisa Cwecwe: So last week I rescued two penguins. The other one was a chick that was underweight and the other one was an adult that was limping. And that adult was nesting and that means it was not able to go to sea to find food for its chicks. …..The other nest I found was an exposed nest so the chicks were wet and freezing. So I had to find brush cut branches and put some cover to protect them. When I went back to check the nest again in the intense rain I found the chicks nice and warm. Erin Bates: So you knew you done well. What’s that feeling like? Yandisa Cwecwe: Like it's a good feeling. It’s a nice feeling. And I followed that nest until the chicks fledged. Don’t mind him, go again UP Beeps sound Erin Bates: There we go. Ok so it’s 11h22. Last three digits 985 Yandisa Cwecwe: 985. So it’s a different bird this week. So the other partner is out foraging. VO15: Competition with commercial fishing boats means adults often can’t find enough food at sea. Yandisa measures the weight and size of the chicks to check they’re getting enough to eat. Yandisa Cwecwe: This is how we hold the chicks because they are still small, we don't want to grab them by their flippers or their legs because they are still fragile. Make sure the chick is away from the face because they can sometimes bite. Erin Bates: Here we go. For the first time I’m holding a penguin. Hello. And how old do you think this one is? Yandisa Cwecwe: It’s two to three weeks old. VO16: Facing starvation, some adults simply abandon their nests. The rest are forced to travel further and further in search of food. UP sound . Erin and Yandisa spots a tortoise “not quite a penguin” VO17 We head to the beach hoping to spot adult penguins returning to land after a long day’s fishing. Yandisa warns us to keep well clear, so we set up our cameras at a distance…and wait. But before heading back to the house, we spot just one penguin reaching shore. Disappointed, we head home for a coffee. Up seagulls sound Erin Bates: Do you feel any connection with the political history of the island? Yandisa Cwecwe: Yah. I took that as a privilege for me to get to robben island and there are still ex political prisoners that still stay on the island that do the prisoner tours. VO18 And while some of her neighbours keep the political legacy alive, Yandisa fights to save its natural heritage ... .sometimes sneaking in a game of netball before bed. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We get a unique glimpse into the life of a female ranger who lives with hundreds of penguins and seabirds on an island whom most of us only remember as a maximum security prison.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Meet Yandisa Cwecwe, Robben Island’s very own penguin and seabird ranger. She has a full time job looking after more than 900 African penguins nesting on the island. Yandisa is the only penguin and seabird ranger stationed on Robben island but from time to time environmentalists and scientists visit the penguin colony to conduct fieldwork and check if the equipment to monitor the penguins’ moves are fully functional.
metadata.Summary: Robben island is situated 11 km from Cape Town harbour. It was declared a marine protected area in 2019 and is managed by Table Mountain National Park. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site best known for its iconic landmark: the maximum security prison where Nelson Mandela and other political prisoners were incarcerated during apartheid. Other iconic landmarks include the Robben Island lighthouse (built in 1864) and relics from WWII when the island was an important military base. But few people know about the penguin colony and for good reason: it is strictly out of bounds for visitors and only a select few are invited to spend a day with these endearing birds in the company of their full time ranger, Yandisa. Yandisa grew up in Lusikisiki in the Eastern Cape, 45 km from the sea. Her interest in marine life and its creatures was sparked during a life-changing visit to a marine protected area along the Eastern Cape Wild Coast. After completing her degree in Zoology she specialised in marine biology. After graduating she worked under the National Research Foundation as a research assistant intern for two years in a Marine Conservation Genomics laboratory at Stellenbosch University before taking up a post at the Southern African Foundation for the Conservation of Coastal Birds (SANCCOB). “My passion and love for the African penguins really began here at SANCCOB where I first worked as a researcher. When the position of ranger became available I immediately applied. I wanted to be on the ground, close to the penguins and other seabirds and to see where they are being rescued. I also wanted to contribute towards the efforts of conserving marine life, especially the endangered African penguin”, says Yandisa. Yandisa’s passion and dedication for her work is evident. Monitoring over a thousand breeding pairs of penguins is no mean feat. Crawling on all fours to check in on the conditions of the newborn chicks or rescuing sick or injured birds, it is all part of a day’s job. “We are always monitoring the chicks on the island especially for being underweight. Penguin food sources have diminished so much due to the overfishing of sardines and anchovies that penguin parents must travel far distances to find food, often leaving their chicks alone for very long periods of time, sometimes not making it back at all. This makes the chicks and eggs vulnerable to predators, bad weather and starvation”, says Yandisa. On average, 500 - 600 African penguin chicks and 300 to 400 African penguin eggs are brought to SANCCOB chick rearing facility at Table Bay each year by rangers from across the 6 penguin colonies with numbers increasing by 256% in the last seven years. The numbers speak for themselves. Abandoned chicks are on the increase and efforts of rangers like Yandisa are critical to the survival of the African penguin. Robben Island is a hotspot for seabird biodiversity, including endangered cape cormorants, bank cormorants and African penguins. It lies in the middle of major shipping lanes, and the risk of oil spills to local seabirds has been well documented. Dr Katta Ludynia, renowned marine biologist, with a Phd spearheads the research department at SANCCOB. She was Yandisa’s mentor whilst being an intern at SANCCOB before she was appointed penguin ranger on Robben Island. She saw Yandisa’s potential if given a chance to prove herself as a ranger and she wasn't disappointed. Katta frequently visits the island to see how the penguins are doing and to see how they can improve the monitoring systems and tools they have in their disposal. The research conducted on the island is critical as it examines the consequences of fishing activities on African penguins and other seabirds’ population dynamics. The research contributes valuable data on the condition of South African seabirds admitted for rehabilitation. Sick or injured birds and abandoned chicks get sent to the mainland Chick Rearing facility where they are then rehabilitated. Shared with research institutions like Earthwatch - an international charity environmental group, these findings play a crucial role in shaping conservation efforts. As part of the national transponder project led by SANCCOB, all released birds are equipped with transponders. For Yandisa, this has been a great two weeks, having enthusiastic people to share her passion with. “The most important thing for me is that I want to contribute towards the efforts of saving endangered marine life especially the african penguins so that is what keeps me going and my passion and love for nature”, says Yandisa. The story: The story is about Yandisa, the penguin ranger and her dedication to help save the penguins. Dr Katta Ludynia, marine biologist working closely with Yandisa will also be on the island to share her concerns for the dwindling penguin population and how they are pulling out all the stops to help preserve this seabird from extinction. We will check the monitoring tools which read the transponders implanted in the penguins, weigh and measure a chicks, check the nests and look for any abandoned chicks or eggs. Katta will also talk about the longstanding penguin project on Robben Island and how the research has given insight into the penguins’ behavioural patterns. We will stay overnight on the island to get early morning and later afternoon shots of the penguins as they go out to sea to forage and return to land to feed their chicks. It is a personal narrative of the penguin ranger and how she spends her life on the island. The science then is a layer on top of that. It becomes more impactful to talk about the impact of climate change, man-made, and the current state of affairs with the penguin population if we have the personal narrative that the viewers can attach themselves to. From thousands of penguins to less than 900 breeding pairs is the reality we face on Robben Island, once the largest breeding colony. Food scarcity, oil pollution and climate change (rise in temperatures, storms, nests flooded) have all contributed. Interviews: Yandisa Cwecwe - Penguin and seabird ranger Dr Katta Ludynia - Marine biologist
metadata.Further information: According to reports from the 1600’s, African penguins were once abundant on Robben Island. However by 1800, they faced so much exploitation and disturbance - primarily for food, clothing, and oil by the early European settlers at the Cape - that they no longer bred there. Not until 1983 did African penguins begin to recolonise Robben Island. After that, the colony grew spectacularly, reaching over 8,000 breeding pairs in 2004 and was briefly the second-largest African penguin colony in the world in 2007. Unfortunately, the story doesn’t end with the penguins’ recovery: the population has declined again. Human activity, such as oil spills and fishing, disturbs their habitat. Not only that, changes in ocean conditions, attributable to the effects of climate change, and the lack of sardine and anchovy - the penguins’ primary food resources - have seen the population plummeting to 1007 breeding pairs. As a result of these collective threats and the continued decline of the penguin populations, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) now classifies the species as Critically Endangered. Decreasing at 7.9% of their population a year, at that rate they could be extinct by 2035.
